title: JavaScript Promises versus Task (same model, different scheduler)
hook: Both models let you write linear async code. The scheduling underneath is not the same: Promises settle into the microtask queue on one JavaScript thread; Tasks resume on a .NET thread-pool thread unless a SynchronizationContext says otherwise.

blocks.text: A JavaScript Promise is a thenable object that is pending, fulfilled, or rejected. A .NET Task is similar in spirit: incomplete, ran-to-completion, faulted, or canceled. await in both languages pauses the current function until the operation completes. But the scheduling differs fundamentally. JS Promise continuations are microtasks that always run on the same JavaScript thread. C# Task continuations may run on any thread-pool thread unless a SynchronizationContext marshals them back.

entries.plainDefinition: JavaScript's built-in async result object. States: pending, fulfilled, rejected.
The .NET reference type representing an async operation. States: running, completed, faulted, canceled.
JavaScript's internal queue for Promise callbacks. Drains before the next macrotask (timers, I/O).
entries.example: Promise.then callbacks always run on the same JS thread.

entries.plainDefinition: JavaScript's cooperative cancellation mechanism. The practical analog of CancellationToken.

blocks.text: Coming from JavaScript, it is tempting to say 'Task is just a Promise.' The programmer model is similar, but the execution engine differs. A long CPU loop in a JS async function freezes the event loop. A long CPU loop in a C# async method after an await still freezes that thread, but other pool threads can proceed. JS has no ValueTask; every async function allocates a Promise. JS has no CancellationToken on the language Promise — AbortSignal is bolted onto fetch and friends.

blocks.title: Interview trap: 'async means parallel'
blocks.body: In both languages, awaiting A then B is sequential. Starting both then combining is concurrent wait. Parallel CPU in JS requires Worker threads; in C# it requires Task.Run or Parallel — neither is what async/await does by itself.

snippet.label: Same composition, different scheduler
snippet.explanation: WhenAll is Promise.all. Continuations may hop threads. In JS, the then callbacks still run on the single JS thread via microtasks.

snippet.label: JavaScript equivalent with Promise.all
snippet.explanation: Same concurrent-wait pattern. Both continuations run as microtasks on the same JS thread after I/O completes.

snippet.label: Cancellation: AbortController vs CancellationToken
snippet.explanation: AbortController is the practical JS analog of CancellationToken, not a hidden field on Promise. Both are cooperative — the operation must observe the signal.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Claiming C# await uses a microtask queue. Using Task.Result in a WhenAll continuation and thinking it is as safe as awaiting. Equating Node worker_threads with C# async/await. Saying 'Task is just a Promise' without noting the different execution engine.

interviewTakeaways: Promise continuations are microtasks on one thread; Task continuations are pool threads unless marshaled.
Promise.all ≈ Task.WhenAll; neither is data parallelism.
AbortController is the practical JS analog of CancellationToken, not a hidden field on Promise.
commonPitfalls: Claiming C# await uses a microtask queue.
Using Task.Result in a WhenAll continuation and thinking it is as safe as awaiting (it is OK after WhenAll completes, but the style hides faults if WhenAll is skipped).
Equating Node worker_threads with C# async/await.

jsTsCorrelations.note: queueMicrotask and Promise.then always run on the JS thread before rendering or I/O macrotasks. Map this against Task continuations that can run on any pool thread.
TypeScript's Promise<T> is a compile-time annotation around a JS Promise. Task<T> is a real CLR type with status, cancellation, and exception storage.
